elements.text: Gemma 4 E4B QAT — Complete Optimization & Testing Guide
Jetson Orin Nano 8GB | Updated September 26, 2026 | Author: Walker Kirkpatrick
Covers: infrastructure optimization (21-config sweep), sampling parameters (51-test sweep), solar games comparison (13/19 games), 48K context testing, and single-shot HTML game prompt design lessons.
1. Hardware & Environment
Platform: NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano 8GB (aarch64, Linux 5.15.199-tegra)
RAM: 8GB unified LPDDR5 (CPU + GPU shared). 7.4GB usable, 5.8GB with GUI off.
Power: Solar-charged Jackery Explorer 500 (100W panel, net 11.30W). 19.6W under load.
Model: Gemma 4 E4B QAT — gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf (4.0GB, Unsloth QAT UD-Q4_K_XL)
Architecture: Dense, 42 layers, 2 KV heads, 256 head_dim, 18 shared KV layers (24 effective), sliding_window 512, 262K vocab. Multimodal (text+image+audio).
Prerequisite: GUI must be OFF before launching model: sudo systemctl stop gdm.service (frees ~1.8GB)
Restart GUI: sudo systemctl start gdm.service
2. Optimized Server Launch Command
This command reflects ALL verified optimizations from the 21-config infrastructure sweep and 51-test sampling sweep:
GGML_CUDA_ENABLE_UNIFIED_MEMORY=1 llama-server \
-m ~/models/gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf \
--alias gemma-4-e4b-qat --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8091 \
-ngl 99 -c 32768 -ctk f16 -ctv f16 \
-b 512 -ub 512 -fa on --jinja --fit off -np 1 -t 6 \
--temp 0.4 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 40 --repeat-penalty 1.0
For 48K context: change -c 32768 to -c 49152 (verified: 17.1 tok/s, 0.28GB margin, zero speed loss)
Launch via setsid (not terminal background wrapper, which adds 200MB overhead and causes OOM):
setsid ~/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server [flags] > logs/server.log 2>&1 &

elements.text: 4.2 Repeat Penalty — Detailed Analysis
repeat_penalty=1.0 (disabled) is the single biggest sampling win: +9% generation speed with zero accuracy loss across all 3 project types.
At rp=1.0: 17.5 tok/s, avg score 98/100
At rp=1.1: 16.0 tok/s, avg score 97/100
At rp=1.15: 15.8 tok/s, avg score 96/100
The speed gain comes from the repeat penalty computation being skipped entirely, reducing per-token overhead.

7. Single-Shot HTML Game Prompt Design Lessons
These findings are derived from 13 solar games + 2 large 48K games = 15 total single-shot HTML game generations.
7.1 CRITICAL: All UI Must Be Canvas-Drawn
The single most important prompt design rule: ALL UI must be drawn on canvas, never split between canvas and DOM/HTML overlays.

Evidence: No Man's Sky prompt said 'draw everything on canvas' — produced a complete playable game (15/16 features). EV Nova prompt allowed HTML overlays for port menus — E4B built the engine (physics, combat, NPCs, audio) solidly but stubbed every menu/transaction screen (trade, outfitter, shipyard, missions all became empty functions with 'omitted for brevity' comments).

Root cause: E4B can implement canvas rendering + game logic in one shot, but cannot implement both canvas rendering AND HTML DOM menu systems in the same output. The split architecture exceeds its single-shot capacity.
7.2 Module Count: 8 Deep > 10 Shallow

8 modules with deep specification produces a more complete game than 10 modules with shallow specification. E4B stops naturally at ~14-15K tokens (finish_reason: stop, not truncated) — it scaffolds architecture but considers the game 'done' before filling in later modules.
7.3 Prompt Sizing for 48K Context
Larger prompts at 48K context work well. E4B produces proportionally larger and more complex output:
48K context has zero speed penalty vs 32K (both f16). The larger context allows larger prompts, which produce larger, more complex games — but module count must stay at 8 to ensure completeness.
7.4 E4B Natural Stop Point

E4B stops generating at ~14-15K tokens with finish_reason: 'stop' — this is NOT truncation. The model considers its work complete. In the EV Nova game, 5 functions are empty stubs with comments like 'Implementation omitted for brevity' — E4B scaffolded the architecture but decided it was done before implementing the transaction/UI layer.

Implication: Design prompts so that all 8 modules can be fully implemented within ~14K tokens. Avoid specifying features that require complex UI flows (trade menus, ship purchase screens) — keep everything canvas-rendered with simple key-triggered actions.
8. OOM Prevention (9 Rules)
1. GDM must be off: sudo systemctl stop gdm.service (frees ~1.8GB RAM)
2. Restart server between EACH game (not every 6) to clear KV cache accumulation
3. Use setsid for long runs, not terminal background wrapper (adds ~200MB, causes OOM)
4. Drop caches between tests: sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches <<< 3
5. -np 1 (single slot): concurrent requests queue. Never run multiple harnesses at once.
6. GGML_CUDA_ENABLE_UNIFIED_MEMORY=1 required for >4GB models on Jetson
7. --fit off required by llama.cpp build 0b1bad1+ (without it, server aborts with -ngl 99)
8. Monitor RAM: free -h before each test. If under 1GB free, stop and restart server.
9. 48K f16 context uses 5.52GB total — only 0.28GB margin. Do not increase to 64K f16 (over budget).
9. Hardened Test Harness Architecture
Three approaches tested for running single-shot game generation on E4B. Reliability improved with each iteration.
9.1 Approach Comparison

rows: Harness dies mid-generation (OOM/gateway cleanup). HTTP connection breaks. Server generates into void. Result lost.
curl as detached subprocess writes to file independently. Harness can parse afterward. Better, but still needs Python process alive to parse.
Server via setsid, curl writes to file, separate Python parser. Each component survives independently. Most resilient.

elements.text: 9.2 Recommended Harness Pattern
1. Launch server via setsid (fully detached from terminal):
setsid llama-server [flags] > logs/server.log 2>&1 &
2. Wait for server with curl health check (not /health — use /v1/models):
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8091/v1/models | grep -q gemma
3. Delete stale response files before each curl:
rm -f logs/response_${NAME}.json
4. Send request via curl with long timeout:
curl -s --max-time 7200 -X POST [endpoint] -d @request.json -o response.json
5. Parse response file with separate Python script after curl completes:
python3 parse_response.py response.json >> results.jsonl
6. Kill server, drop caches, proceed to next game
9.3 Critical Harness Rules
- Delete stale response files before each curl (race condition: old file parsed as 0 tokens)
- Ensure only one curl at a time against single-slot server (-np 1)
- sync_caches needs sudo: subprocess.run(['sudo','tee','/proc/sys/vm/drop_caches'], input=b'3\n')
- Resume logic: check completion_tokens > 0 AND no error key to count as completed
- Server restart between EACH game prevents KV cache accumulation crash
10. Code Quality Review Findings
Deep code review of 13 solar game HTML outputs + 2 large 48K game outputs.
10.1 Solar Games (13 outputs reviewed)

12 of 13 games are clean code: well-formed HTML, balanced braces/parens/brackets, zero external dependencies, zero TODO/FIXME markers, no duplicate functions. All have canvas rendering, Web Audio API sound, and game loops.
1 bug found in 13 games: Checkers Duel (game 9) had a duplicate executeMove function and win condition never checked. 92% clean code rate.
10.2 EV Nova (detailed review)

Root cause: E4B built a solid space combat engine (physics, combat, NPCs, audio) but ran out of output budget before implementing the menu/transaction layer. The game has empty updateTrading, updateShipUpgrades functions — E4B scaffolded the architecture but did not fill in the interactions.
